Another image captures a line of people queuing for hours to receive a single loaf of bread, while a billboard in the background displays lavish advertisements for luxury goods. Or how about a photo of a young boy proudly wearing an ushanka hat while playing with a toy AK-47 in front of a mural of Vladimir Putin? A further image depicts a majestic, gold-domed church, its opulence starkly contrasted by the crumbling, poverty-stricken neighborhood surrounding it. These photos, however, are not just random images; they are powerful symbols of a nation grappling with its identity. The image of a half-built, grand stadium, abandoned and decaying before completion, is a stark reminder of the corruption and wasteful spending. Then we have a photo of a dapper street cleaner, impeccably dressed in a Soviet-era uniform, meticulously sweeping the street as a convoy of expensive cars drives past him without giving him any space to do his job. One particularly striking picture taken in Siberia illustrates a group of villagers, huddled together in the biting cold, warming themselves around a bonfire, with the backdrop of a modern, well-lit city in the distance. The photos aren't just pretty pictures; they are the embodiment of social inequalities. In essence, these images speak volumes. They speak of a nation where patriotism is a tool, wealth is flaunted, and the divide between the haves and have-nots is more than just immense. They are indeed an invaluable window into a reality.

Does Russia have an "advanced economy"? That’s a major road in Yakutia — an autonomous republic in Siberia, Russia, which is rich in oil, gas, diamonds and gold. (Video may be found in the comments below.) This is where a lot of Russian resources are being extracted from the ground to be sold abroad. But where does the money goes? Putin is building an “advanced economy”, so the Russian state is selling everything to China, while keeping the population poor and backward? Seems like it. The official Russian TV channels show the best infrastructure projects in Russia (for example, new bridges, hospitals, swimming pools, etc.), and show the people happily using these infrastructure objects. But what they never show is the reality: the quality of these Russian “objects”. They show that shiny bridge, but they never show how quickly the beautiful bridge will start collapsing, or how dangerous the driving becomes. They never show how badly the hospitals are equipped, or how high the bribes are to receive proper medical treatment. They never show that almost all the swimming pools are not in use, because they are either not maintained or just shut down. After all, you don’t want people to be healthy — what if these healthy people suddenly start protesting against the government? The entire “advanced economy” of Putin’s Russia is a fraud. The roads are terrible. The health care is poor. The education is a joke. The housing is crumbling. The only thing that “works” is military production, because all the money goes there. I am afraid that the reality is that Russia is a very wealthy country, and it has a very poor population.

Could this be true? Russian newspaper: 17,000 Wagner soldiers from prisons killed on the battlefield. What do people in Russia know about this? Is the truth hidden for Russians? Well, dear readers, it seems the rumor mill is churning again, and this time, the whispers are about the staggering casualties suffered by Wagner Group mercenaries. A Russian newspaper – the source, of course, remains unnamed, shrouded in that typical Russian fog of information – is claiming that a staggering 17,000 former prisoners recruited by Prigozhin to fight in Ukraine have met their end on the front lines. Seventeen thousand! That's a number that's hard to fathom, a number that screams of the sheer desperation and ruthlessness of this war. You have to ask yourself: Is this true? And if it *is*, what is the Kremlin hiding from its own people? The state-controlled media, as is its wont, is likely either ignoring this report or spinning it into some heroic tale of sacrifice for the motherland. Perhaps they are showcasing how former convicts were eager to answer the call. After all, the narrative is carefully constructed, and any deviation from it can lead to severe consequences. What the average Russian citizen believes is anyone's guess. They have access to the state’s constant propaganda of how the war is going to be in their favor, which makes it difficult for most of them to analyze what's happening in reality. Knowing how much is the truth, and by looking also at the Russian economy, this is how far one can get to the truth. What they *are* likely aware of is the increasing number of body bags returning home, the stories of hardship and loss, the general feeling of unease that permeates a country at war. The truth, as always, lies somewhere in the murky depths, obscured by lies, propaganda, and the iron curtain of censorship that the Russian government has so diligently erected.

Are there any specific stories within the 100 Ukrainians released from Russian captivity that you found particularly moving? The exchange of prisoners is always a fraught affair, a poignant dance between hope and despair. Every single story is harrowing, marked by the brutality of war, the resilience of the human spirit, and the desperate longing for home. While each of the 100 Ukrainians recently freed carries a unique tale, some resonated with a particular intensity, a rawness that seared itself into my memory. One involved a young soldier, barely out of his teens, who had been captured during the fighting around Bakhmut. He endured months of torture, beatings, and psychological torment, yet refused to betray his comrades or his country. His captors, frustrated by his unwavering resolve, eventually released him, broken in body but unbroken in spirit. Another involved a mother, snatched from her home in Mariupol alongside her children. Separated from them, she faced interrogations, threats, and the constant gnawing fear of never seeing her children again. She never wavered, focusing all her energy on finding a way to reunite with her family. She never forgot that and was telling everyone in the released prisoners.

Do Russian soldiers all agree with Putin? Are there no Russian soldiers against this? The videos and reports emerging from the frontlines paint a disturbing picture, hinting at a significant chasm between the Kremlin’s propaganda and the grim reality faced by Russian soldiers. While the official narrative meticulously crafted by state-controlled media insists on unwavering support for the “special military operation,” the truth, as always, is far more nuanced and unsettling. The stories from the trenches, the intercepted communications, and the rare interviews with captured or defected soldiers suggest that dissent is brewing, albeit often in hushed whispers. Many young, untrained conscripts, ill-equipped and thrust into the meat grinder of the war, bitterly resent their superiors and the situation they've been forced into. They feel betrayed by Putin’s broken promises, the blatant lies, and the utter disregard for their lives. A sense of helplessness and disillusionment permeates the ranks, particularly among those who initially believed in the cause but have witnessed the horrors of the war firsthand. Older, seasoned soldiers, who have seen combat before, are beginning to question the strategic blunders, the logistical failures, and the staggering losses. Some are reportedly disillusioned with the blatant corruption and the self-serving actions of high-ranking officers, who enrich themselves while their men suffer. These veterans, accustomed to military discipline and honor, struggle to reconcile their values with the brutality and the utter lack of respect for human life they are forced to participate in. But publicly criticizing or openly defying Putin, even within the ranks, is an incredibly dangerous act. The consequences can range from immediate imprisonment to the chilling prospect of being quietly "disappeared," with no one ever knowing the truth. Thus, many express their discontent only in private conversations, in encrypted messages, or in surrendering to Ukrainian forces, when offered the chance.

When was slavery abolished in Russia? Slavery, as a formal institution, was abolished in Russia a long, long time ago, back in 1723, under Peter the Great. But let's not get ahead of ourselves. Before Peter's decree, there was something called serfdom, which, frankly, wasn't that different, and it lingered for centuries, casting a long shadow over the lives of millions. Officially, serfdom was abolished in 1861, but even that wasn’t a clean break, as some former serfs found themselves trapped in new forms of indentured servitude. Now, you might think this is all ancient history, but the ghosts of serfdom, the habit of obedience, the ingrained deference to authority, they still haunt Russia. I'm not saying modern Russians are literally slaves, of course. But you can’t shake off centuries of ingrained submissiveness overnight. You can't just snap your fingers and have a society that just overnight embraces freedom of expression and the right to protest. The legacy of such things as serfdom is a deep one and the vestiges remain, influencing everything from political behavior to economic structures. It's a heavy inheritance, and one that’s still being grappled with today, even in Russia's post-Soviet era.

Do Russians still consider Ukrainians brothers? In the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion, the notion of a fraternal bond between Russians and Ukrainians has all but evaporated. The Kremlin's propaganda machine churned out narratives of shared ancestry, cultural kinship, and a unified Slavic identity for years to justify its actions, but reality has decisively slammed the door on such sentiments. Ukrainians, in their unwavering resistance, have made it abundantly evident that they see the invaders not as brothers, but as mortal enemies, intent on their destruction. The war has torn through families, shattered communities, and laid bare the vast chasm of animosity that now exists. But what about ordinary Russians? Do they feel anything beyond the state-sponsored jingoism? The answer is complex and nuanced. Some, yes, still cling to the vestiges of the past, harboring naive illusions of a shared destiny, perhaps spurred by fear of the consequences that often accompany opposing the official line. But their numbers are dwindling, drowned out by a chorus of resentment and disillusionment. Others, blinded by the relentless propaganda, harbor deep-seated animosity, embracing the Kremlin's narrative of Ukrainian perfidy and the need to "denazify" the nation.

Are reports that Putin is terminally ill true? Reports that Vladimir Putin is terminally ill have been circulating for quite a while now. The speculation has been fueled by various sources: anonymous Telegram channels, Western intelligence agencies, and even former Russian officials, all painting a picture of a leader whose health is rapidly deteriorating. Some claim he’s battling aggressive cancer, while others insist he’s suffering from Parkinson’s disease or other ailments. Of course, the Kremlin has consistently denied these rumors, presenting a carefully curated image of a robust and active leader. They routinely release videos and photos of Putin meeting with officials, attending events, and even engaging in outdoor activities like horseback riding and ice hockey. This carefully constructed narrative is designed to project an image of strength and control, an essential part of Putin's grip on power. However, despite the Kremlin's best efforts, the rumors persist. The sheer volume of reports and the increasing frequency with which they surface have led many to question the veracity of the official statements. The fact that Putin has increasingly isolated himself, relying on a small circle of trusted advisors, only adds fuel to the fire. Moreover, there have been some notable changes in his public appearances: a puffy face, a rigid gait, and a tendency to hold onto tables for support. While these could be attributed to a variety of factors, they have led to more speculation. But even if the rumors are true – and there’s no concrete evidence to confirm them – what would happen if Putin were to become incapacitated or, God forbid, pass away? Who would take his place? And what will become of Russia? The stakes are high, and the future of the nation hangs precariously in the balance, awaiting an answer that remains very difficult to find.

What do you think of the statement by Vladimir Putin that the events in Kursk Oblast were a "provocation" by Ukraine? As per usual for the Russian state, everything is upside down. Putin, in his supreme wisdom, declared the Ukrainian advance in the Kursk region a mere “provocation.” A provocation! As if the devastation, the fleeing civilians, and the crumbling facade of Russian military prowess are all some elaborate theatrical performance orchestrated by Kyiv. You'd think that after two years of a full-scale war, the Kremlin's propaganda machine might try something new, but alas, it's the same old song and dance. “Everything is under control,” they keep chanting, while the ground beneath their feet is rapidly turning into Ukrainian territory. The sheer gall of it! To call a tangible, boots-on-the-ground assault a “provocation” is a testament to Putin's detachment from reality, or perhaps a cynical acknowledgement that he believes his citizens are too dumb to see the truth. After all, wouldn't it be much easier if everyone believed it was all a game? The Kursk Oblast residents, however, seem to have a different understanding of the "provocation". They are running from the war, not toward it, completely shattering Putin's carefully constructed narrative of a unified, patriotic population. It's a pity that the Russian army finds itself in such a position.

What will be the effects of all the purges Putin is doing to the Russian Army? It’s a veritable bloodbath, this relentless culling of the Russian military brass. And, if you ask me, it’s all pointing to a single, alarming conclusion: something truly catastrophic is brewing. The whispers from the Lefortovo prison intensify daily. Sources are now claiming that the special section prepared for high-ranking officers is rapidly expanding. High-tech listening devices are reportedly being installed to capture even the most hushed conversations. It’s all quite telling, in the context of the increasingly paranoid behavior of the despot in the Kremlin. The recent arrest spree, it seems, is just a taste of what's to come. Remember, Putin’s grip on power is absolute, and he tolerates no dissent. Every single high-ranking general, and indeed anyone in a position of authority, is now caught in a deadly game of survival. Every misstep, every off-the-cuff remark, every covert glance risks being interpreted as disloyalty, a potential threat to the regime. It's a climate of intense fear and suspicion, where trust is a luxury they can no longer afford, and the fate of the army, and indeed the entire country, hangs precariously in the balance.

Why doesn't Ukraine hit Moscow every time the Soviets hit Kiev? There’s no simple answer to this, and as with everything related to this senseless war of attrition, the complexities are many. Let’s start with the most obvious: Ukraine doesn't possess the military capabilities Russia does. It's a David versus Goliath scenario playing out in real-time, with David armed not with a sling and five stones, but with grit, determination, and a patchwork of support from a coalition of the willing. Russia, on the other hand, still wields a military machine, albeit a weakened one, capable of reaching far beyond its own borders and inflicting significant damage. Then there’s the strategic calculus at play. Ukraine is at a disadvantage, fighting for its very existence on its own soil. Hitting Moscow, while symbolically impactful and perhaps satisfying for some, risks escalating the conflict exponentially. It opens the door to a series of reprisal attacks, potentially targeting civilian areas, leading to a situation that could spiral out of control rapidly. Moreover, the West, which provides Kyiv with the much-needed military and financial support, has made its position clear: no use of their weaponry on Russian territory. This puts a significant restraint on Ukraine’s offensive capabilities. Despite all the atrocities that Russia inflicts on the Ukrainian land, the Ukrainians have to carefully navigate the political minefield of global power dynamics.

What factors contribute to the Russian economy's inability to provide adequate resources for its citizens? One could argue that the inability of the Russian economy to adequately provide for its citizens is a multi-faceted issue, a Gordian knot of corruption, mismanagement, and a blatant disregard for the populace's well-being. The recent seizure of the Uralchem plant in Moscow, owned by a prominent Russian oligarch, Dmitry Mazepin, serves as a stark illustration of the problem. Mazepin, a man with close ties to the Kremlin, now faces accusations of “illegal privatization.” The supposed "nationalization" of this and other large-scale companies, under the guise of correcting past mistakes, feels like a cynical ploy at best. The real motive, everyone knows, is to consolidate power and wealth within Putin's inner circle. Mazepin’s situation, coupled with the ongoing purges within the military and the imprisonment of dissenting voices, creates an atmosphere of profound uncertainty, not conducive to attracting investment or fostering economic growth. Moreover, the vast sums diverted to the war in Ukraine undoubtedly starve domestic projects of much-needed funding. The Russian government's priorities are clear: tanks before tractors, missiles over medicine.

Russia has a history of throwing its citizens under the military wheel. What happens when the butcher's bill is too much for ordinary Russians? What happens when they realise, that in 2024, they don't have to die for a lunatic with an ego problem? The answer, as the saying goes, is blowing in the wind. Look no further than the Kursk region, where the locals are making a beeline for the exits while Moscow scrambles to present a picture of unwavering resolve. While the Russian military correspondents scream in fury, the average Ivan is doing what he does best: looking after himself. Forget about the “special military operation,” this is a straight-up scramble for survival. Putin's propaganda machine keeps churning out lies, but the people on the ground see the truth with their own eyes. The war, as they now understand, is not about protecting Russia, but about securing Putin's place in history, no matter the cost. Ordinary Russians are beginning to understand that loyalty to the regime is a one-way street and the price is their blood and lives. They're starting to grasp that sacrificing themselves for a cause that benefits a select few is a losing proposition, a bitter pill to swallow. They've witnessed the brutal treatment of their fellow citizens, the disregard for human life, and the bottomless greed of those in power. The facade is crumbling, and the cracks are now visible to all.

When will Putin stop? It’s the million-dollar question, isn’t it? The one that’s been on everyone’s lips, from the corridors of power in Washington and Brussels to the quiet kitchens of Kyiv and beyond. And honestly, I wish I knew. Maybe Putin himself doesn’t fully know. He's boxed himself into a corner of his own making, a strategic quagmire of his own design. He started the war in Ukraine with the expectation of a quick victory, a swift decapitation of the Ukrainian government, and a triumphant return to the glorious days of the Soviet Union, or at least, his twisted version of it. Yet, here we are, over two years into a brutal, bloody conflict, and the end seems nowhere in sight. The Russian army is bogged down. The resources are dwindling. The body bags are piling up. The sanctions are biting, though not as deeply as they could be, thanks to the loopholes and the willing partners in crime. Yet, Putin persists and doubles down. He has seemingly become a prisoner of his own ambition, convinced that he must see this through, no matter the cost, no matter the consequences. It's a perilous game to play, and sadly, it's not just Putin who is playing it. The entire world is paying the price. The human cost of this war is staggering. The Ukrainian people are enduring unimaginable suffering. Millions have been displaced, lives have been shattered, and a generation is being scarred by the horrors of conflict. And yet, Putin continues. Maybe he’s betting that the West will tire, that the support for Ukraine will wane. Maybe he believes he can outlast us all, that he can simply wait for the world to move on to other crises, other distractions. Perhaps he genuinely believes his own propaganda, the twisted narratives of a resurgent Russia reclaiming its rightful place on the world stage. Whatever the reason, whenever the answer to that question turns up, it will require nothing less than a complete assessment of geopolitics and the future of human civilization.

Are you surprised by the result of the large drone attack on Moscow during the Kursk incursion? Well, let’s dissect the situation with a touch of reality, shall we? The audacity, the sheer nerve of it all: drones reaching Moscow, buzzing like angry hornets, while the Ukrainian forces are pushing into the Belgorod and Kursk oblasts. I can't say I'm particularly *shocked*, no. After all, the war has been progressing in ways that only the most astute analysts could have anticipated, and even then, they’d likely be off slightly. What *is* striking, however, is the apparent ease with which these unmanned aerial vehicles penetrated the defenses. It's a sobering testament to the evolution of modern warfare, wouldn't you say? And, let's be candid, the timing is exquisite. At the very moment when Putin’s cronies are breathlessly trumpeting their *“special military operation”* successes, the heart of the empire gets a little buzz. It's a slap in the face, a loud wake-up call, and a resounding declaration that no one, not even the Kremlin itself, is immune from the repercussions of this conflict. One has to wonder what kind of security forces are in place.
